extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students covering court and police news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporters on gathering, selecting, and writing court-related news (police court, criminal trials, civil suits, probate, appeals) to be published in newspapers. Emphasizes selection of significant details, fairness, avoidance of sensationalism, and clear attractive presentation without sacrificing accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of story (scope of court news)
rubrics_metrics.description: All forms of judicial procedure are included under court news; stories of this class cover such matters as police court news, criminal trials, civil suits, divorce suits, bankruptcy, wills and other probate court matters, decisions of higher courts, and findings of judicial officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since much court news is routine, the matter-of-fact informative news story is a frequent medium for presenting it, but selecting salient and significant phases can make even routine court news interesting to casual readers (cf. examples cited: 'Supreme Court Decision', 'Criminal Court', 'Municipal Court', 'Forgery Case').

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: fair and accurate publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: To give fair and accurate publicity to significant phases of the administration of justice; court proceedings are activities of important branches of government and hence are matters of public concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer's aim should be to inform the public responsibly; constructive reporting of crime and trials serves public knowledge and the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of details (reader-centered significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reporting sessions of these bodies, the writer's aim should be to direct the reader's attention to those details of the proceedings (1) that are significant to him personally, (2) that affect the interests of the community, and (3) that relate to the welfare of society as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and emphasize facts that meet one or more of the three criteria above to make the story relevant and meaningful to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism and morbid emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Destructive, or anti-social, influences are found in those court stories—particularly those of criminal and divorce cases—that play up disgusting or scandalous phases of such trials in order to gratify the morbid taste of some readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not emphasize salacious or revolting details merely to attract attention; such treatment is harmful to public interest and journalistic ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'try the case in the newspaper'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid publishing news stories and editorials before or during a trial that attempt to prove the innocence or guilt of an accused person by printing whatever evidence can be secured, even though some of it would be excluded from the trial under the rules of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from printing inadmissible evidence or editorializing in a way that creates public opinion likely to prevent the accused from receiving a fair trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of material: clarity and attractive presentation without sacrificing accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: To find matters of general significance and interest, particularly when they are buried in legal technicalities and verbiage, and to present them clearly and attractively without sacrificing accuracy, are the main problems in handling court news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to translate legal technicalities into clear prose, highlight salient points, and make the story appealing while maintaining factual precision; this is challenging but worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop human-interest elements appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal and civil cases often have a strong human interest element that, if rightly developed, may be a valuable part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human-interest angles (the 'little comedies and tragedies' of police court) to engage readers, but develop them responsibly and in service of the facts and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style choice for routine court news
rubrics_metrics.description: Since much court news is of a routine character, the matter-of-fact informative news story is a frequent medium for presenting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a straightforward, informative style for routine matters, but do not assume such stories must be dry—bring out salient and significant phases to maintain reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity as a deterrent (social function of court reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The wide-spread publicity given by newspapers to the punishment inflicted on wrong-doers tends to deter others from similar illegal acts, and thus aids in accomplishing the chief object of punishment ('The wages of sin is publicity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the social impact of court reporting; constructive stories of crime that responsibly report punishment can contribute to deterrence and public understanding.
